title: -able, -ible, and -ness
objectives: I can use the endings -able and -ible to understand describing words.
I can use the ending -ness to understand nouns that name a feeling or quality.
I can find the base word in each word and explain what the ending adds.
I can write sentences that use words from this unit correctly.
rationale: Suffixes turn words students already know into the abstract adjectives and nouns of grade 4 reading. Here the endings -able and -ible (able to be) and -ness (state or quality) are taught through ten words with a visible base (flex, predict, reverse, adjust, avail, fair, aware, willing, lonely) and one with a root (edible). Students learn the spelling changes at the seam (drop the e in reverse, change y to i in lonely). The unit reuses dependable, convenient, and durable from earlier units as examples of the same pattern, and the passage uses a school garden club to show how the words describe objects, plans, and feelings.

words.def: Able to bend easily without breaking.

senses.example: We kept our plans flexible in case it rained.

words.ex: A flexible plastic ruler bends without snapping.
words.ex2: A gymnast must be flexible to bend into a full split.
words.nonExample: A frozen board that snaps in half is not flexible.

apps.academic: In science, a flexible material can bend without breaking.
apps.spoken: I'm flexible about when we meet.
apps.writing: Use flexible for things that bend, and for people who change plans easily.

cloze.s: The gymnast was so ___ that she could bend backward and touch her head with her toes.

cloze2.s: Rubber bands are ___, so they stretch and then bounce back to their shape.

misuse.s: The flexible board snapped in two the moment she touched it.

visual.alt: A gymnast bending beside a stretchy ribbon.

words.def: Easy to guess before it happens.
words.ex: The ending of the cartoon was predictable because it always ended the same way.
words.ex2: Sunrise is predictable; it happens every morning.
words.nonExample: A surprise party is not predictable.
words.rel: things we can know or use

apps.academic: In science, tides are predictable because they follow a pattern.
apps.spoken: The weather isn't very predictable today.
apps.writing: Use predictable for events you can guess from a pattern.

cloze.s: After watching three episodes, Kai found the plot ___ and could guess every twist.

cloze2.s: Tides are ___ because scientists can tell when the water will rise and fall.

misuse.s: The surprise party was predictable because nobody guessed what would happen.
misuse.why: Predictable means easy to guess; a surprise nobody guessed is not predictable.

words.def: Able to be turned the other way or changed back.
words.ex: My reversible jacket is blue on one side and red on the other.
words.ex2: Freezing water into ice is reversible because the ice can melt back into water.
words.nonExample: Burning a log into ash is not reversible.

morph.note: The final e of reverse is dropped before -ible.

apps.academic: In science, melting is a reversible change.
apps.writing: Use reversible for things that can turn over or go back to how they were.

cloze.s: Her ___ coat is red on the outside and blue on the inside, so she can wear it two ways.

cloze2.s: Dissolving sugar in water can be ___: when the water dries up, the sugar comes back.

misuse.s: Burning the log into ash is reversible because the ash can turn back into a log.
misuse.why: Reversible means it can be changed back; ash cannot become a log again.

visual.alt: A jacket beside a circle of arrows.

words.ex: The park ranger taught us which wild berries are edible.
words.ex2: Many flowers are pretty, but only some are edible.

morph.note: From a Latin word meaning to eat.

words.rel: things we can know or use

apps.academic: In science, some plants are edible, and some are poisonous.
apps.writing: Use edible for things that people can safely eat.

cloze.s: Only a few of the mushrooms in the forest are ___, so never taste one without an expert.

cloze2.s: The cake had flowers on top, and every one of them was ___.

misuse.s: The shiny rocks are edible, so we cooked them for dinner.
misuse.why: Edible means safe to eat; rocks are not.

visual.alt: A strawberry beside a fork and knife.

src.note: The root ed (eat) is from Latin; keep for human review.

words.def: Able to be changed a little to fit.
words.ex: The chair has an adjustable seat, so it fits both of us.
words.ex2: An adjustable wrench can open wide or close tight to fit any bolt.
words.nonExample: A shirt sewn in one size is not adjustable.

apps.academic: An adjustable microscope lets scientists focus on tiny details.
apps.writing: Use adjustable for things that can be changed to fit a person or a job.

cloze.s: The bike seat is ___, so it can be raised for taller riders.

cloze2.s: A watch with an ___ strap can fit a small wrist or a large one.

misuse.s: The ruler was adjustable because it was glued in one position forever.
misuse.why: Adjustable means it can be changed; glued forever means it cannot.

words.def: Ready to be used, bought, or reached.
words.ex: Fresh strawberries are available at the market in June.
words.ex2: The principal is available to meet with parents after school.
words.nonExample: A book checked out by someone else is not available.
words.rel: things we can know or use

apps.academic: The library keeps many books available for students.
apps.writing: Use available for things or people that you can use or reach right now.

cloze.s: The doctor is ___ to see patients every day except Sunday.

cloze2.s: All the red bikes were sold, so only blue bikes were ___.

misuse.s: The last ticket was available, even though it had been sold hours ago.
misuse.why: Available means ready to be bought or used; a sold ticket is not available.

visual.alt: A check mark beside a price tag.

words.def: Knowing about something that is happening around you.
words.ex: Her awareness of the storm helped her bring the dog inside early.
words.ex2: Posters at school raise awareness about recycling.
words.nonExample: Being asleep and not noticing is not awareness.

apps.academic: Campaigns raise awareness of health and safety.
apps.spoken: I have more awareness of the problem now.
apps.writing: Use awareness for knowing about something or noticing it.

cloze.s: The campaign raised ___ of litter in the park and got students to pick it up.

cloze2.s: A hiker's ___ of the snake in the grass kept her from stepping on it.

misuse.s: Her awareness of the noise was so strong that she never noticed a sound.
misuse.why: Awareness is knowing about something; never noticing means no awareness.

words.def: Treating everyone in a way that is equal and right.
words.ex: The judge was praised for her fairness to both teams.
words.ex2: Fairness means everyone gets a turn on the swing.
words.nonExample: Giving one student extra time and no one else is not fairness.

apps.academic: In a debate, fairness means each side gets the same time to speak.
apps.writing: Use fairness for treating people equally and right.

cloze.s: The coach showed ___ by giving every player the same amount of time on the field.

cloze2.s: Dividing the pizza into equal slices was a sign of ___ among the friends.

misuse.s: Fairness means one person gets all the treats and everyone else gets none.

visual.alt: A balance scale beside a handshake.

words.def: Being ready and glad to do something.
words.ex: Her willingness to help made her a favorite teammate.
words.ex2: The class showed its willingness to try by raising every hand.
words.nonExample: Refusing to try is not willingness.

apps.academic: A student's willingness to try again is part of learning.
apps.spoken: Thank you for your willingness to help.
apps.writing: Use willingness for being glad and ready to do something.

cloze.s: Her ___ to share her lunch with a new classmate made him feel welcome.

cloze2.s: Tom showed great ___ when he volunteered to clean the whole room by himself.

misuse.s: His willingness to help was clear when he refused to lift a finger.
misuse.why: Willingness is being glad to help; refusing is the opposite.

visual.alt: A raised hand beside a thumbs-up.

words.def: The sad feeling of being alone.
words.ex: Loneliness crept in when Sam moved to a town where he knew no one.
words.ex2: A friendly note can ease a classmate's loneliness.
words.nonExample: Playing happily with friends is not loneliness.

morph.note: The y in lonely changes to i before -ness.

apps.academic: Stories often show how a character overcomes loneliness by making a friend.
apps.spoken: I felt loneliness when I moved.
apps.writing: Use loneliness for the sad feeling of being alone.

cloze.s: After her best friend moved away, ___ filled the long afternoons.

cloze2.s: The explorer felt ___ during months at sea with no one to talk to.

misuse.s: He felt loneliness at the crowded party because he was laughing with all his friends.
misuse.why: Loneliness is the sad feeling of being alone; laughing with friends is the opposite.

visual.alt: A person standing alone in the rain.

passage.title: Maya and the Garden Club
paras: On her first day at the new school, Maya felt a wave of loneliness. Everyone seemed to know each other already, and the hallway buzzed with voices she did not know. Then she noticed a sign: "Garden Club, all students welcome."

Mr. Ortiz, the club leader, showed Maya around the garden. "We have a few jobs available," he said. "Our schedule is flexible, so you can help whenever you like." He handed her an adjustable trowel, a small shovel with a handle that could be made longer or shorter.

The students grew many plants. Some were edible, like lettuce and cherry tomatoes, and some were only for color. A girl named Ana explained the rules. "Fairness matters here," she said. "Everyone gets a turn with the best tools." Maya was glad. She had hoped no one would be left out.

As the weeks went by, Maya grew in awareness of her classmates. She noticed who liked to water and who liked to dig. Her willingness to try new jobs impressed everyone. Even the weather became predictable: a sunny morning meant the lettuce would need water by noon.
On the last day, Mr. Ortiz gave each student a reversible apron, green on one side and yellow on the other. Maya wore it with the green side out. She no longer felt alone.

qs.q: In paragraph 3, what does the word "edible" mean?
qs.why: Lettuce and cherry tomatoes are foods, so edible means safe to eat.

choices: Able to be made longer or shorter
qs.why: The next phrase says the handle could be made longer or shorter.

qs.q: Why did Maya feel glad when Ana talked about fairness?
choices: She wanted the best tools for herself.
She hoped no one would be left out.
She wanted to leave the club.
She planned to win a prize.
qs.why: Maya had hoped that no one would be left out, and fairness means everyone gets a turn.

qs.q: Which detail shows that Maya no longer felt lonely at the end?
choices: She joined the Garden Club on the first day.
Mr. Ortiz gave her a trowel.
She wore the apron and no longer felt alone.
qs.why: The story says she no longer felt alone.

qs.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Joining a club helped a lonely new student feel welcome.
Gardens grow best in the sun.
Mr. Ortiz is a strict teacher.
qs.why: Maya starts out lonely and ends feeling that she belongs.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words that use the endings -able, -ible, and -ness. They find the base word, name what the ending adds, and notice spelling changes such as dropping the e in reverse and changing y to i in lonely. The garden-club story shows the words in use.

notes.va.flexible.adj: Flex + -ible. Show a ruler and a stick. The second sense of changing plans easily is useful in school: a flexible plan. Students often write flexable.
notes.va.predictable.adj: Predict + -able. Link to science predictions. Ask students to predict what comes next in a pattern and say the word.
notes.va.reversible.adj: Reverse drops the e before -ible. Connect to reversible changes in science, such as melting. Students sometimes confuse reversible with reverse.
notes.va.edible.adj: Ed means eat, from Latin. Students often write edable. Sort a few real foods and non-foods on the board.
notes.va.adjustable.adj: Adjust + -able. Show an adjustable strap or chair. Ask where students see adjustable things at school.
notes.va.available.adj: Avail + -able. Link to available in the school library. Students often confuse available with free; it means ready to use or reach.
notes.va.awareness.n: Aware + -ness. Awareness is abstract; use a short example of noticing a hazard. Contrast with attention.
notes.va.fairness.n: Fair + -ness. Connect to classroom rules. Ask students for a time when something was fair and a time when it was not.
notes.va.willingness.n: Willing + -ness. Ask students to name actions that show willingness, such as raising a hand to help.
notes.va.loneliness.n: Lonely + -ness, with y changing to i. Handle with care: some students may be lonely. Focus on how people help each other.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'I see awareness. The base word is aware, which means knowing about something. The ending -ness turns an adjective into a noun for the state of being aware. So awareness is the state of knowing about something.'

misconceptions: Every word ends in -able; there is no -ible.

teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit the suffixes two days later by asking students to add endings to five new bases. At one week, add dependable, convenient, and durable from earlier units to the chart.
